Q: find successor in AVL tree A:

Key idea: In-order traversal visits nodes exactly in ascending sorted order. So if you remember the last node you visited (call it prev), then the moment you visit a new node curr, you know for certain that curr is the successor of prev.

You don't need a parent field, and you don't need a LinkedList/array — the only "extra memory" used is the recursion call stack (which is implicit, not a data structure you build yourself), plus one pointer variable (prev).

Pseudocode:

Node prev = null;  // global / outer-scope variable

void findSuccessors(Node node) {
    if (node == null) return;

    findSuccessors(node.left);      // go left first

    if (prev != null) {
        // we now know prev's successor: it's the current node
        print(prev.value, "-> successor is", node.value);
    }
    prev = node;                    // current becomes "previous" for the next visit

    findSuccessors(node.right);     // then go right
}

Call findSuccessors(root) once. At the end, whatever node was last set to prev (the maximum value in the tree) simply has no successor (null) — which is correct, since the max element has nothing after it.

Why this works without parent pointers: the recursion itself implicitly "remembers the path" back up the tree for you — that's exactly the information a parent pointer would have given you, except it's encoded in the call stack instead of in the node.

Complexity:

  • Time: O(n) — you visit every node exactly once.

  • Space: O(h) where h is the tree height (call stack depth) — for an AVL tree, h = O(log n), so this is quite efficient. No auxiliary collection needed.

Bonus — if you want truly O(1) extra space (no recursion/stack at all):
There's a technique called Morris Traversal. It temporarily turns the tree into a "threaded" structure: for each node, it finds the rightmost node in its left subtree (its in-order predecessor) and makes that predecessor's right pointer temporarily point to the current node. That thread is the successor link. As traversal proceeds, these temporary threads are used to get back up the tree without a stack, and then removed (restoring the original tree) once used. It's more intricate to implement correctly, but it's the standard answer when even O(log n) recursion space isn't allowed.

Q: How to wait for a WebSocket's readyState to change A:

I just read all the answers and there is only one right solution because WebSockets and the WebSocket server are designed that way.

  • Some answers use "polling". You spoil computer power with that.

  • The only right answer is using "events".

When you begin with a new WebSocket, the new WebSocket will fire an "open" event when it has an connection with the WebSocket server. You need to handle that event. From this event you can start sending "messages" to the Websocket server and you may assume the connection is "open". The Websocket server sends those "messages" to other connected WebSockets. You subscribe to those "messages" with an message handler.

Q: How to code a Linux kernel module? A:

You are missing the module_init() and module_exit() macros and some crucial #defines. We need more information as well such as your make/gcc options. It may be reporting the "invalid module format" because you are compiling in 32bit when your kernel is 64bit, so ensure you are using the -64 compile and link flag.

A great hello world tutorial for Kernel Modules is located here.

Welcome to writing kernel modules. They are a lot of fun compared to writing Windows drivers (I've done both). The linux kernel module interface is much simpler to use and there is a lot of base drivers you can delegate to and get the work done faster.

Q: ImportError: cannot import name 'AgentExecutor' from 'langchain.agents' A:

The AgentExecutor import error is expected behavior if you're on LangChain 1.0+ — AgentExecutor, along with create_tool_calling_agent and create_react_agent, was removed from the core package in that release. Here's how to fix it, depending on what you actually want to do.


## Check your version first

pip show langchain

Option 1 (recommended): Migrate to create_agent

LangChain replaced AgentExecutor with a new high-level API built on LangGraph's runtime:

from langchain.agents import create_agent

agent = create_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",  # or "openai:gpt-4o", etc.
    tools=[search_tool, wiki_tool, save_tool],
)

response = agent.invoke({
    "messages": [
        {"role": "user", "content": "your query here"}
    ]
})

This is the actively maintained path going forward. It gives you the same "just call .invoke()" simplicity as AgentExecutor, but it's a LangGraph graph under the hood, so it also supports things AgentExecutor never did cleanly — e.g. persistent memory across turns via a checkpointer:

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

agent = create_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",
    tools=[search_tool, wiki_tool, save_tool],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)

config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "some-id"}}
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}, config=config)

Option 2: Keep the old API working

The deprecated agent classes weren't deleted outright — they were moved into a separate package:

pip install langchain-classic

from langchain_classic.agents import AgentExecutor, create_tool_calling_agent

This lets old tutorials/code keep running with a minimal change, but it's not where new development is happening — worth treating as a stopgap while you migrate.

Why this happened

LangChain and LangGraph both hit a 1.0 milestone, with a stated commitment to no breaking changes until 2.0. The old AgentExecutor loop was a black box that didn't flex well for streaming, custom control flow, or multi-agent setups — create_agent exposes the same simple interface for the common case while being built on LangGraph's graph model, so you can drop into more complex control flow later without switching frameworks.

References:

  • LangChain 1.0 agents docs
  • LangChain & LangGraph 1.0 release notes
